head.title: Health tracking that works offline, with no account.

head.statement: Privacy-first doesn't mean feature-poor. Guest Mode plus offline-first architecture delivers a premium UX with zero account friction.

rows.v: Most fitness apps demand an account before you can log anything, keep your data on their servers, and stop working the moment you lose signal.
Built a local-first tracker on IndexedDB with opt-in cloud sync, on-device macro calculations, and forecast states that admit when the data cannot support a prediction.
Making offline-first feel premium, and deciding what a forecast should say when it genuinely does not know.

blocks.html: Most fitness apps share one flaw: they want an account before you can do anything. Your data lives on their servers, behind their subscription, under their privacy policy. For anyone privacy-conscious, or just not ready to commit before trying, that's a dealbreaker.
The second problem: they're cloud-dependent. No internet means no access to your own history.
The core decision was to make IndexedDB the primary data layer instead of a remote database. That means:

items: The app loads and works instantly. No auth, no network request, no spinner.
Everything lives on the device by default.
Supabase sync is opt-in, and only kicks in when you create an account.

blocks.html: I used Dexie.js as the IndexedDB wrapper for its clean promise-based API and live query hooks that re-render React components when data changes. It behaves like Supabase's real-time, but fully offline.

blocks.text:
Guest Mode  →  IndexedDB only  →  Zero account friction
Sync Mode   →  IndexedDB + Supabase  →  Multi-device access

blocks.html: Switching from Guest to Sync migrates your local data to the cloud, so nothing is lost. You get to try the whole product before committing to anything.

images.alt: Form dashboard: weight, BMI, and trend with goal and average reference lines

blocks.caption: Weight, BMI, and a trend line reading from local IndexedDB, before a single account exists.

blocks.html: Daily weight logs stored locally, with BMI calculated automatically. The trend chart uses Recharts with a custom gradient fill and reference lines for goal weight and rolling average.
A naive forecast engine will happily tell a plateauing user "goal in 4,000 days." Forecasts fail in predictable ways, so I turned each failure into a designed state:

items: Not enough data (under 7 days): asks you to keep logging instead of guessing
Plateau (under 0.01kg/day change): called out honestly as stagnant, not projected forward
Off track (trending away from goal): flagged plainly instead of showing a receding date
Unrealistic horizon (over 730 days): reads "Long Term Goal" instead of a fake-precise date

blocks.html: The forecast earns trust precisely because it admits when it shouldn't be trusted.

Macro targets are calculated on the device with the Mifflin-St Jeor BMR formula. No third-party nutrition API, no cloud round-trip, all in keeping with the privacy-first architecture. Inputs: weight, height, age, gender, activity level, goal. Output: daily calories, protein, carbs, and fat in grams.

images.alt: Form daily targets: on-device calorie and macro calculation

blocks.caption: Calories and macros calculated on-device with Mifflin-St Jeor. No API round-trip, no cloud dependency.

blocks.html: Waist, chest, hips, and arms tracked over time, since scale weight alone is a poor read on body composition.
Optional sync with Google Fit through its API, so Form slots into an existing health setup instead of replacing it.
Full data portability. Import history from other apps (if they export CSV) and export your Form data whenever you like. No lock-in.

Building local-first made me treat data ownership as a design constraint, not just a technical one. Every schema decision had to answer two questions: what happens when this data needs to sync, and what happens when local and remote disagree?

The Guest/Sync split also taught me that cutting friction at the top of the funnel beats adding features. In early testing, the biggest driver of retention was letting people start tracking without an account.
Privacy-first doesn't mean feature-poor. Guest Mode plus offline-first gives you a premium experience with zero account friction.
